title: Broad Street to Bunhill Fields: the Visions of Albion
register: national mythology, the canon is true

segments.name: Broad Street and the First Visions

stops.name: Broad Street, Soho, the birth
stops.campa: William Blake is born over his father's hosier's shop at 28 Broad Street, Soho, third surviving child of James Blake and Catherine Hermitage Blake. The street is loud with tradesmen's cries and looms southward toward the fields that still edge London. He is christened at St James's, Piccadilly, a few days on. Nothing yet marks the house as different from its neighbors, but the boy who will see angels in these rooms and this small garden is already breathing London's coal-smoke air, and already, his family will later say, unlike other children from the first.
suggested_refs: The baptismal register of St James's Piccadilly, 11 December 1757
28 Broad Street (now Broadwick Street), the birthplace site
sources: Oxford Dictionary of National Biography, 'Blake, William'

stops.name: Broad Street, God at the window
stops.campa: A small boy of four looks up and God puts His head to the window and screams, and the child screams too, in terror at the nearness of it. This is the first of the visions, told afterward by the family as the plain truth of what happened in that upstairs room, not a dream reported at breakfast but a visitation that frightened a small child badly enough to be remembered a lifetime. No one in the house on Broad Street has seen anything like it before or since. The boy does not forget the shape of that face at the glass.
suggested_refs: Gilchrist's account of the vision at the window, Life of William Blake, ch. 1
sources: Gilchrist, Life of William Blake (1863), ch. 1

stops.name: Peckham Rye, the tree filled with angels
stops.campa: Walking out to Peckham Rye, still open country south of the river, the boy of eight looks up into an oak and sees it filled with angels, their wings bespangling every bough like stars. He runs home and tells it plainly, as a thing seen. His father, a hard practical man, is ready to thrash him for lying; only his mother, Catherine, stands between them and saves him the beating. The vision is never retracted. Decades later Blake will still name Peckham Rye as the place where Heaven first opened over an English common.
suggested_refs: The Blake Society plaque near Goose Green, Peckham Rye
Samuel Palmer's letter recalling Blake's account of the tree of angels
sources: Gilchrist, Life of William Blake (1863), ch. 1

stops.name: Henry Pars' Drawing School, the Strand
stops.campa: James Blake, seeing that his son's gift will not be argued out of him, spares the ordinary schooling and sends the boy of ten instead to Henry Pars' drawing school in the Strand, to copy from plaster casts of antique statuary. His father gives him small sums to buy prints at the auction houses, and the boy comes home with engravings after Raphael, Michelangelo, Dürer and Marten Heemskerck, poring over them instead of playmates. He is already forming the taste, half-Gothic and half-antique, that will set him against every fashionable painter of his century.
suggested_refs: Blake's boyhood print collection, later dispersed
The plaster casts of Pars' academy in the Strand
sources: Gilchrist, Life of William Blake (1863), ch. 2

stops.name: Great Queen Street, apprenticed to James Basire
stops.campa: At fourteen, too old-fashioned in his tastes for the fashionable painter Blake's father first proposed, the boy is bound apprentice for seven years to James Basire, engraver to the Society of Antiquaries, at his shop in Great Queen Street. Here he learns the plain, hard, linear discipline of the burin, unlike the softer stipple then coming into vogue, a discipline he will call, all his life, the true and correct line against the blotting and blurring of the moderns. Basire is a sound and honest master. The trade Blake is given here will still be feeding him at his death.
suggested_refs: James Basire's engraving shop, 31 Great Queen Street
Blake's indenture of apprenticeship, 4 August 1772
sources: Society of Antiquaries of London, archive notes on Basire's apprentices

stops.name: Westminster Abbey, the opened tomb of Edward I
stops.campa: Basire, wanting to separate his quarreling apprentices, sends young Blake alone into Westminster Abbey to draw the royal monuments for Richard Gough's Sepulchral Monuments. On the second of May the antiquaries open the tomb of Edward I, dead four hundred and fifty years, to examine the body within, and Blake is set to record it. He climbs among effigies of Henry III, Queen Eleanor, Queen Philippa, Edward III, Richard II, spending whole days alone in the vaulted quiet, the Gothic line entering his hand so deeply that it will outlast every fashion he is ever asked to imitate.
suggested_refs: Blake's drawings of the Westminster Abbey tombs, Society of Antiquaries collection
Richard Gough, Sepulchral Monuments in Great Britain (1786, 1796)
sources: Society of Antiquaries of London, exhibition notes on Blake's Abbey drawings

stops.name: Westminster Abbey, the vision of Christ and the Apostles
stops.campa: Alone in the long aisles among the tombs he is set to copy, the light falling through the clerestory, Blake sees the aisles filled: Christ walking among his twelve Apostles, a great procession of monks and priests behind them, and hears their chant rise into the vaulting as if the stones themselves were still singing the offices ended centuries before. It comes to him here as plainly as the Abbey's own carved stone, unbidden, while his pencil is still on the paper. He does not ask whether it is a granted grace or a common one; he only draws, after, more surely.
suggested_refs: Blake's later biblical illustrations, drawing on this Abbey vision of procession and chant
sources: Gilchrist, Life of William Blake (1863), ch. 2

stops.name: Westminster Abbey, the quarrel with the Westminster schoolboys
stops.campa: The boys of Westminster School, let into the Abbey on old privilege, find the solitary apprentice on his scaffold an easy mark and taunt him at his drawing until one goes too far. Blake, no lover of being trifled with even as a boy, knocks him down from the scaffold to the pavement below. He goes at once to the Dean to lay his complaint rather than wait to be blamed, and the Dean, hearing him out, withdraws the schoolboys' privilege of the Abbey entirely. The vaulted aisles are quiet again, and Blake's solitary hours among the Gothic dead resume undisturbed.
suggested_refs: The Dean of Westminster's withdrawal of the schoolboys' access, recorded in Blake's early biographies
sources: Gilchrist, Life of William Blake (1863), ch. 2

stops.name: Old Somerset House, Royal Academy student
stops.campa: His apprenticeship out, Blake enters the Royal Academy schools at Old Somerset House as a student, free of fee but bound to find his own materials for six years. He falls in at once with John Flaxman, Thomas Stothard and George Cumberland, sharing their radical politics as freely as their studios, and comes to admire the fierce independence of Fuseli and James Barry over the polished manner Sir Joshua Reynolds, the Academy's president, holds up as law. Blake sets Michelangelo and Raphael's hard clean line against Reynolds's oil-shadowed fashion, and never afterward troubles to hide his contempt for the Academy's taste.
suggested_refs: Blake's Royal Academy student registration, 8 October 1779
Blake's marginalia against Reynolds's Discourses
sources: Myrone, 'William Blake as a Student of the Royal Academy', Blake/An Illustrated Quarterly

stops.name: St Mary's Church, Battersea, the marriage
stops.campa: Nursing a heartbreak from a woman who refused him, Blake tells the whole sorry story to a gardener's daughter called Catherine Boucher and her family in Battersea. When he asks her, 'Do you pity me?' and she answers that she does, he declares on the spot, 'Then I love you,' and within the year marries her at St Mary's, Battersea, on the eighteenth of August. Catherine, unable to read or write, signs the register with her mark. Blake will teach her to read, to draw, to color his plates and pull his prints, and she will outlive him only four years, faithful to the end.
stops.quote: Do you pity me? ... Then I love you.
stops.quote_source: Recounted in Gilchrist, Life of William Blake (1863), of Blake's proposal to Catherine Boucher, 1781-82
suggested_refs: The marriage register of St Mary's, Battersea, 18 August 1782, signed with Catherine's mark
sources: Gilchrist, Life of William Blake (1863), ch. 3
britannica.com, 'William Blake: Marriage to Catherine Boucher'

stops.name: Broad Street, Poetical Sketches printed
stops.campa: Friends of the household, chiefly the Reverend Anthony Stephen Mathew and the sculptor Flaxman, put up the money to have Blake's early verses set in ordinary type and printed as Poetical Sketches, the only book of his ever produced by a conventional press rather than his own hand. The poems, some written as young as twelve, already carry the plain, singing, half-archaic diction that will run through everything he writes after. He will never again trust a printer with his words; from here the page itself becomes something he must make, not merely fill.
suggested_refs: Poetical Sketches (1783), Blake's only conventionally typeset book
sources: Gilchrist, Life of William Blake (1863), ch. 4

stops.name: Broad Street, the print shop and the father's death
stops.campa: James Blake dies in July, and William, with his old schoolfellow James Parker, opens a print-selling shop next door to the family home at 27 Broad Street, taking his younger brother Robert in as an assistant and pupil. Robert, gentle and gifted, has followed William's own hand and eye almost from birth, and the two work the counter and the graver together. It is a hard trade in a hard year, but the brothers are close in a way William will not be close to any other living soul, and the shop keeps them under one roof daily.
suggested_refs: 27 Broad Street, the print shop kept with James Parker and Robert Blake
sources: Gilchrist, Life of William Blake (1863), ch. 5

stops.name: Broad Street, the death of Robert
stops.campa: Robert sickens of consumption and William nurses him without sleep for the last fortnight, sitting at the bedside until his own body gives out with exhaustion and grief. At the moment of death William sees, plain before him, his brother's released spirit rise up through the plain matter-of-fact ceiling of the room, clapping its hands for joy at the moment of its release. It is not sorrow alone he carries out of that room but a fact: that the body's ending is not the spirit's, seen with his own eyes, in his own house, over his own brother.
stops.quote_source: Blake's own account of Robert's death, recorded in Gilchrist, Life of William Blake (1863), ch. 6
suggested_refs: Robert Blake's burial, Bunhill Fields, February 1787
sources: Gilchrist, Life of William Blake (1863), ch. 6

stops.name: Poland Street, Robert's spirit teaches the secret of illuminated printing
stops.campa: A year after the death, Robert comes again, not clapping now but teaching: in a vision, William's dead brother shows him the whole method he has been groping toward, a way of writing his poems and drawing his designs together directly on copper in a liquid that resists the acid, so that when the plate is etched the words and images stand up in relief, ready to print, while all else bites away. Blake rises the next morning, buys the materials the vision named, and it works exactly as shown. Illuminated printing, and with it the illuminated books, are given him this way, complete.
suggested_refs: The relief-etching process of illuminated printing, as revealed and used from 1788 onward
sources: Gilchrist, Life of William Blake (1863), ch. 6

stops.name: Poland Street, Songs of Innocence printed
stops.campa: With the method Robert gave him, Blake etches, prints, and with Catherine hand-colors the first copies of Songs of Innocence: the Piper on the hill who lays down his pipe at a child's request and writes his happy songs in a book that all may read, the Lamb, the Chimney Sweeper's dream of an Angel with a bright key. Each copy is a unique object, no two colored quite alike. He is at once author, engraver, printer and illuminator of his own book, a whole trade folded into one man and one household, exactly as the vision on Broad Street promised.
stops.quote: Piping down the valleys wild, / Piping songs of pleasant glee, / On a cloud I saw a child, / And he laughing said to me: / 'Pipe a song about a Lamb!'
suggested_refs: Songs of Innocence (1789), illuminated copies hand-colored by William and Catherine Blake
sources: The William Blake Archive, Songs of Innocence

stops.name: Hercules Buildings, Lambeth, the workshop of prophecy
stops.campa: The Blakes move south of the river to a larger house in Hercules Buildings, Lambeth, with room enough for a press and a garden Blake is said to sit naked in with Catherine, reading Paradise Lost aloud to a startled visitor, unashamed as Adam and Eve. Here for a decade he will print nearly all his great illuminated books. The French Revolution has just broken out across the water; Blake wears the bonnet rouge in the London streets in sympathy, and begins, on these presses, to build in verse and copper a whole answering mythology of England's own fall and promised redemption.
suggested_refs: Hercules Buildings, Lambeth, Blake's home and workshop 1790-1800
sources: Gilchrist, Life of William Blake (1863), ch. 9

stops.name: Lambeth, The Marriage of Heaven and Hell
stops.campa: At the Lambeth press Blake etches The Marriage of Heaven and Hell, and a Devil, called to account in the Memorable Fancies, answers the Angel not with apology but with scripture of his own, printed in the infernal method, by corrosives, which in Hell are salutary and medicinal, melting apparent surfaces away and displaying the infinite which was hid. The Voice of the Devil declares Energy the only life, and Reason its outward bound; the Proverbs of Hell are read out plate by plate as the Devil's own gospel, and Blake gives it to the reader as fact, not fable.
stops.quote: The road of excess leads to the palace of wisdom. ... Energy is Eternal Delight.
stops.quote_source: The Marriage of Heaven and Hell, 'The Voice of the Devil' and 'Proverbs of Hell' (c. 1790-1793)
suggested_refs: The Marriage of Heaven and Hell, plates 4-10, the Proverbs of Hell
sources: The William Blake Archive, The Marriage of Heaven and Hell

stops.name: Lambeth, Visions of the Daughters of Albion and America a Prophecy
stops.campa: Two prophetic books come off the Lambeth press in the same season. In Visions of the Daughters of Albion, Oothoon, ravished and chained by Bromion, cries out against every law that binds desire, and Blake gives her cry the standing of scripture. In America a Prophecy, the fiery rebel Orc, chained beneath the Atlantic, rises against the tyrant Albion's Angel and the war for the colonies is refought as the first eruption of the energy that Urizen's cold laws had bound down. The mythology of a fallen and warring Albion, invented whole in this house, is now fully launched.
stops.quote: The soul of sweet delight can never be defiled.
stops.quote_source: Visions of the Daughters of Albion, plate 8 (1793)
suggested_refs: Visions of the Daughters of Albion (1793) and America a Prophecy (1793)
sources: The William Blake Archive, Visions of the Daughters of Albion; America a Prophecy

stops.name: Lambeth, Songs of Experience and the Book of Urizen
stops.campa: Blake binds Songs of Experience to Songs of Innocence as the two contrary states of the human soul, the Tyger burning against the Lamb, the Sick Rose against the blossoming one. In the same year The First Book of Urizen gives the mythology its dark demiurge entire: Urizen, the cold self-shut architect of law and measurement, exiled from the other Eternals, sets his compasses over the void and begins to build the fallen world of rule and limit. Blake etches him full length in the frontispiece, an ancient bearded lawgiver dividing the darkness with an instrument, the enemy the whole prophetic corpus will now answer.
stops.quote: Tyger Tyger, burning bright, / In the forests of the night, / What immortal hand or eye / Could frame thy fearful symmetry?
suggested_refs: Songs of Innocence and of Experience (1794 combined edition)
The First Book of Urizen (1794), the frontispiece of Urizen with his compasses
sources: The William Blake Archive, Songs of Innocence and of Experience; The First Book of Urizen

stops.name: Lambeth, Europe a Prophecy and the fall of Albion
stops.campa: Europe a Prophecy carries the mythology across the Channel: Enitharmon, Albion's fallen female portion, casts her false sleep of eighteen centuries over the earth while Los, the eternal prophet and smith, labors at his furnaces against her, and Orc's fire finally breaks out as the French Revolution across the water. The frontispiece shows the Ancient of Days himself leaning from a burning disc of sun, dividing the deep with golden compasses, an image Blake will color and recolor to his last years, the fallen creator caught in the very act of drawing the limit he cannot see beyond.
suggested_refs: Europe a Prophecy (1794), frontispiece: 'The Ancient of Days'
sources: The William Blake Archive, Europe a Prophecy

stops.name: Lambeth, Vala, or The Four Zoas begun
stops.campa: Blake begins the vast unillustrated manuscript he first calls Vala and later The Four Zoas, an attempt to gather the whole scattered mythology, Urizen, Luvah, Tharmas, Urthona and his emanations, into a single epic of the fall and eventual resurrection of the primeval man Albion, of whom England and every reader is a fallen member. He writes it on the backs of proof sheets for Edward Young's Night Thoughts, revising for years without ever engraving it whole or letting it go to press. It is the deepest working of the private scripture, and it will never, in his lifetime, leave the manuscript state.
suggested_refs: Vala, or The Four Zoas, manuscript, British Library
sources: The William Blake Archive, Vala or The Four Zoas

segments.name: Felpham, the Cottage by the Sea

stops.name: Felpham, the cottage by the sea
stops.campa: At the invitation of the poet William Hayley, who promises a year's steady work and the run of his library, Blake and Catherine move down from London to a thatched cottage at Felpham on the Sussex coast, the only long exile of his life from the city that made him. He writes to Flaxman within days that heaven opens here on all sides her golden gates, that voices of celestial inhabitants are heard more distinctly and their forms seen more clearly than ever in London's smoke, and that his old friends the Villagers of Felpham, ordinary rustic figures, appear to him now as gods of the mountains and the sea.
stops.quote: Felpham is a sweet place for study, because it is more spiritual than London. Heaven opens here on all sides her golden gates... voices of Celestial inhabitants are more distinctly heard, & their forms more distinctly seen.
suggested_refs: Blake's Cottage, Felpham, now preserved by the Blake Cottage Trust
sources: Blake's Cottage Trust, 'Blake and the Cottage'

stops.name: Felpham, Milton's shade enters Blake's foot
stops.campa: Walking in the garden at Felpham, Blake sees the dead poet John Milton descend as a falling star out of the zenith, swift as a swallow, and enter him bodily through the left foot at the tarsus, a visitation he will set down whole in the epic he calls simply Milton. The elder poet has come, the poem says, to correct the errors of his own theology and to redeem his sixfold emanation, and the living poet's body becomes, for the length of the vision, the very ground the dead one walks to be healed. Blake writes for years afterward inside that entered foot.
stops.quote: Then first I saw him in the Zenith as a falling star, / Descending perpendicular, swift as the swallow or swift; / And on my left foot falling on the tarsus, entered there.
stops.quote_source: Milton, a Poem, plate 15 (composed and etched 1804-1810, the vision set at Felpham)
suggested_refs: Milton, a Poem, plate 15, the falling star entering Blake's foot
sources: The William Blake Archive, Milton a Poem

stops.name: Felpham, the letter of the fourfold vision
stops.campa: Writing to his patron Thomas Butts back in London, Blake sets down in verse, plain as a letter home, the whole ladder of his seeing: single vision, the flat sleep of Newton and Locke that most men never wake from; twofold vision, always granted him; threefold, the soft vision of Beulah's night; and fourfold, his own supreme delight, in which the world stands open all the way to Eternity at once. He asks God to keep him from ever falling back to single sight, as if it were a soul's true danger, worse than any illness Felpham's damp air can give him.
stops.quote: Now I a fourfold vision see, / And a fourfold vision is given to me; / Tis fourfold in my supreme delight / And three fold in soft Beulahs night / And twofold Always. May God us keep / From Single vision & Newtons sleep!
suggested_refs: Blake's letter to Thomas Butts, 22 November 1802, the fourfold-vision verses

stops.name: Felpham garden, the fairy's funeral
stops.campa: Alone one evening in the cottage garden, Blake hears a pleasant sound he cannot at first place, and looking closer sees a procession of small creatures, the size and color of green and grey grasshoppers, carrying a body laid out upon a rose-leaf. They bury it with songs too fine for a human ear to hold entire, and then vanish as if the hedge had simply closed over them. He tells it afterward exactly as he saw it, a fairy's funeral witnessed the way another man might witness a neighbor's, and never troubles to soften the report for a listener's disbelief.
stops.quote: A procession of creatures of the size and colour of green and grey grasshoppers, bearing a body laid out on a rose leaf, which they buried with songs, and then disappeared.
stops.quote_source: Blake's account as recorded in Allan Cunningham, Lives of the Most Eminent British Painters, Sculptors and Architects (1830)
suggested_refs: Allan Cunningham's account of the fairy's funeral at Felpham
sources: Cunningham, Lives of the Most Eminent British Painters (1830)

stops.name: Felpham garden, the soldier Scofield
stops.campa: A private soldier named John Scofield, billeted at the Fox Inn, wanders drunk into Blake's garden and refuses to leave when told; words rise, and Blake, no small man and roused past patience, takes him by the collar and elbows and marches him bodily the fifty yards down the lane to the inn where he is quartered, before witnesses enough to matter later. Scofield, humiliated, swears out an information that Blake damned the King and called the soldiers all slaves, a charge of sedition in a year when invasion barges are said to be massing across the Channel and every such word is weighed as treason.
suggested_refs: The indictment of William Blake, 1803, West Sussex Record Office (QR/W643)
sources: West Sussex Record Office, 'The Indictment of William Blake, 1803'

stops.name: Chichester Guildhall, the trial for sedition
stops.campa: Bound over by the Petworth magistrates, Blake stands trial at the Chichester Guildhall, once the great church of the Priory, before a jury in a coastal county thick with troops and invasion fear, on Scofield's charge that he cried down the King and called every soldier a slave. Hayley stands surety and testifies to his character; the case against him is thin and full of holes, and the jury acquits him outright, to applause in the courtroom. He walks free of the charge that could have hanged him, but the fright of it, and the county's suspicion of the visionary in its midst, hastens the Blakes' return to London within the year.
suggested_refs: Chichester Guildhall (the former Priory church), site of the 1804 trial
sources: West Sussex Record Office archive blog

segments.name: South Molton Street, the Silent Years

stops.name: South Molton Street, the return to London
stops.campa: Shaken but unbowed by the Felpham ordeal, the Blakes take rooms at 17 South Molton Street, Mayfair, where they will stay eighteen years. Hayley's steady patronage is over, and with it the last regular income Blake will ever again enjoy; he returns instead to jobbing engraving work, illustration commissions that pay little and come seldom, and his own unsold, unread prophetic books. He begins here to write Milton and to expand the vast manuscript of Jerusalem, working now for a public he has almost entirely lost, in a city that has already half-forgotten the young engraver's early promise.
suggested_refs: 17 South Molton Street, Blake's home 1803-1821
sources: Gilchrist, Life of William Blake (1863), ch. 20

stops.name: South Molton Street, 'And did those feet in ancient time'
stops.campa: In the short preface to Milton, Blake sets down sixteen lines that ask whether the holy Lamb of God was ever seen on England's mountains green, whether Jerusalem was builded here among these dark satanic mills, and vows that he will not cease from mental fight nor let his sword sleep in his hand till a new Jerusalem is built in England's green and pleasant land. Almost unread in his lifetime, the verses will one day be set to music and sung in cathedrals and at the last night of the Proms as the nation's second anthem, its author dead in poverty and obscurity a century before anyone thinks to ask his name.
stops.quote: And did those feet in ancient time / Walk upon England's mountains green? / And was the holy Lamb of God / On England's pleasant pastures seen?
stops.quote_source: Milton, a Poem, Preface (composed c. 1804-1808, etched 1810)
suggested_refs: Milton, a Poem, Preface, later set by Hubert Parry as the hymn 'Jerusalem' (1916)
sources: The William Blake Archive, Milton a Poem

stops.name: Broad Street, the 1809 exhibition
stops.campa: Cheated of a commission to illustrate Chaucer's Canterbury Pilgrims by the dealer Robert Cromek, who hands the subject instead to Stothard, Blake mounts his own rival exhibition above his brother James's hosiery shop at 27 Broad Street, sixteen works only, with a Descriptive Catalogue as much manifesto as guide. The single published notice, in The Examiner, calls the pictures wretched daubs, the catalogue a farrago of nonsense and vanity, and the artist himself an unfortunate lunatic whose harmlessness alone keeps him out of confinement. No pictures sell. Blake will not exhibit publicly again in his lifetime.
suggested_refs: A Descriptive Catalogue of Pictures (1809)
Robert Hunt's review, The Examiner, 17 September 1809

stops.name: South Molton Street, Jerusalem completed
stops.campa: After sixteen years of writing and engraving, Blake completes and begins to print copies of Jerusalem: The Emanation of the Giant Albion, the longest and most fully worked of his illuminated books, one hundred plates telling the fall of Albion, the primeval and universal man in whom England and all mankind are one body, and his slow redemption through the imaginative labor of Los. Blake calls it the grandest poem that this world contains, and offers, at its close, to lead any reader who takes hold of it by a golden string wound into a ball straight in at Heaven's gate, built in Jerusalem's wall.
stops.quote: I give you the end of a golden string; / Only wind it into a ball, / It will lead you in at Heaven's gate, / Built in Jerusalem's wall.
suggested_refs: Jerusalem: The Emanation of the Giant Albion, complete illuminated copies (1820)

stops.name: South Molton Street, John Linnell
stops.campa: Introduced by the engraver George Cumberland's son, the young landscape painter John Linnell calls on Blake, now over sixty, poor and nearly forgotten, and finds not a broken man but a mind undimmed, still full of designs. Linnell will become the second great patron of Blake's life after Hayley, buying and commissioning steadily through the last years, drawing a circle of young admiring artists around the old visionary's chair, and, by simple faithful payment, keeping Blake and Catherine from real want in the years when almost no one else in London remembers his name.
suggested_refs: John Linnell's diary entries recording his introduction to Blake, 1818
sources: Gilchrist, Life of William Blake (1863), ch. 26

stops.name: Fountain Court, the Strand, the last home
stops.campa: The Blakes give up South Molton Street for two small rooms at 3 Fountain Court, off the Strand, in the house of Catherine's brother-in-law. It is a poor lodging, but the Thames is close, and the rooms are filled, visitors will remember, with an atmosphere of ease and quiet purpose that has nothing of squalor in it despite the poverty. Here, at a plain table by the window, Blake will do nearly all his last and greatest work, Catherine always within call, mixing colors, stretching paper, guarding the door against callers when the work will not bear interruption.
suggested_refs: 3 Fountain Court, the Strand, Blake's last home 1821-1827
sources: Gilchrist, Life of William Blake (1863), ch. 27

stops.name: Fountain Court, the engravings for the Book of Job
stops.campa: Linnell commissions a full set of engravings illustrating the Book of Job, and Blake, who has drawn Job's sufferings and restoration in watercolor for patrons before, now cuts twenty-two plates entire: Job and his family in the false comfort of outward piety at the start, the whirlwind and the voice out of it, Job's daughters at the end hearing him tell of the visions he has seen. It is the last complete, finished work of his life, engraved with a controlled clarity that even hostile critics will later have to grant, when almost nothing else of his was yet allowed to be great.
suggested_refs: William Blake's Illustrations of the Book of Job (engraved 1823-1826, published 1826)
sources: en.wikipedia.org, "William Blake's Illustrations of the Book of Job"
The William Blake Archive, Illustrations of the Book of Job

stops.name: Fountain Court, the Divine Comedy watercolours begun
stops.campa: Linnell sets Blake to a hundred and one designs illustrating Dante's Divine Comedy, and Blake, who has never read Italian and works from a borrowed translation, throws himself into Dante's Hell, Purgatory and Paradise as into a country he already half knows: Minos coiling his tail in judgment, the whirlwind of the lustful, Dante and Virgil among the ice. He tells his young friends plainly that Dante saw devils where he himself sees none, that Dante was, for all his genius, a mere politician busied with this world as Milton had been, until old age turned him back at last to the God he had known in childhood.
suggested_refs: Illustrations to Dante's Divine Comedy, 102 watercolours and unfinished engravings (1824-1827)
sources: themarginalian.org, 'William Blake's Breathtaking Drawings for Dante's Divine Comedy'
tate.org.uk, 'William Blake's illustrations to Dante's Divine Comedy'

stops.name: Shoreham, Kent, the young disciples, the Ancients
stops.campa: A small circle of young painters, Samuel Palmer, Edward Calvert, George Richmond and Frederick Tatham among them, gather around the old man in his last years, walking out from London to visit him at Fountain Court and retreating themselves to the secluded valley of Shoreham in Kent, which they come to call, half in joke and half in earnest, their own Eden. They call themselves the Ancients in honor of his unfashionable, antique-loving art, and carry his visionary method of pastoral England, seen double, into their own generation's work long after his own name has been let fall by the wider world.
suggested_refs: Samuel Palmer's Shoreham 'valley of vision' sketches, made under Blake's influence

stops.name: Fountain Court, the last day and the death
stops.campa: Blake works at the Dante drawings until his strength gives out, then turns to Catherine, in tears at his bedside, and asks her to stay just as she is so that he may draw her portrait once more, for she has ever been an angel to him; he finishes it, lays down his tools, and begins to sing. His friend George Richmond, sent for, later writes that he died in a most glorious manner, saying he was going to the country he had all his life wished to see, and just before the end his countenance grew fair, his eyes brightened, and he burst out singing of the things he saw in Heaven.
stops.quote: Stay, Kate! Keep just as you are — I will draw your portrait — for you have ever been an angel to me.
stops.quote_source: George Richmond's account, recorded in Gilchrist, Life of William Blake (1863), ch. 36

stops.name: Bunhill Fields, the burial
stops.campa: Five days after his death, William Blake is carried to the Dissenters' burying ground at Bunhill Fields and laid in unconsecrated ground not far from his brother Robert, in a grave he shares, unmarked at the time, with strangers above and below him, as was the custom of the poor. Catherine, faithful past the end, tells visitors in the years remaining to her that William still comes and sits with her of an evening and advises her on her work. No stone marks the exact spot for a century; when one is finally raised, it will carry his own words: Jerusalem's wall.
suggested_refs: Blake's grave, Bunhill Fields, marked with a memorial stone in 1927 (relocated 2018)
sources: Gilchrist, Life of William Blake (1863), ch. 36
